PICK A TOPIC AND DISCOVER NATO Language selection Close Menu Member countries Basic points Key events Activities Working structures Member countries The most important players in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization are the member countries themselves, called NATO Allies. There are currently 32 members Sort: Alphabetically By accession date NATO membership is open to “any other European state in a position to further the principles of this Treaty and to contribute to the security of the North Atlantic area.” A political and military alliance NATO’s purpose is to guarantee the freedom and security of its members through political and military means. POLITICAL – NATO promotes democratic values and provides a permanent structure for its members to consult and cooperate on defence and security-related issues. Regular consultation enables NATO members to share their views, exchange information, build trust, solve problems and, in the long run, prevent conflict. MILITARY – NATO is committed to the peaceful resolution of disputes. However, if diplomatic efforts fail, it has the military power needed to defend every one of its members – as stated in Article 5, the collective defence clause of NATO's founding treaty. It can also undertake crisis management operations to help preserve peace and stability on the international stage, alone or in cooperation with other countries and international organisations. Collective defence The bedrock commitment at the core of NATO is that an attack against one of its members is considered as an attack against all. This is the principle of collective defenceopens in a new tab, which is enshrined in Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. In a spirit of solidarity, NATO Allies will come to each other’s assistance when needed. So far, Article 5 has been invoked only once – in response to the 9/11 terrorist attacks in the United States in 2001. The transatlantic link NATO is an alliance of countries from Europe and North America. It provides a unique link between these two continents, enabling its members on both sides of the Atlantic to consult and cooperate in the field of defence and security, stand in solidarity and deter aggression from potential adversaries, and conduct multinational crisis management operations together. The 2022 Strategic Concept Strategic Concepts set out NATO’s core tasks and principles, its values, the evolving security environment, and its strategic objectives for the next decade. The most recent Strategic Conceptopens in a new tab, agreed in 2022, reaffirms that NATO's key purpose is to ensure the collective defence of its members, based on a 360-degree approach, and outlines three core tasks – deterrence and defence, crisis prevention and management, and cooperative security. Explore NATO History opens in a new tab 19491989199119952001200320142022 THE BIRTH OF NATO AND THE COLD WAR EUROPE REUNITED NATO AFTER 9/11 RENEWED FOCUS ON COLLECTIVE DEFENCE Activities Every day, NATO member countries consultopens in a new tab and take decisions on security issues, at all levels and in a variety of fields. All decisions at NATO are taken by consensusopens in a new tab. A “NATO decision” is therefore the expression of the collective will of all 32 member countries. Hundreds of officials, as well as civilian and military experts, come to NATO Headquarters each day to exchange information, share ideas and help prepare decisions when needed, in cooperation with national delegations and the staff at NATO Headquarters. NATO is a defensive alliance. Its core purpose is to safeguard the freedom and security of its member countries and their one billion people. NATO members keep each other safe and secure by maintaining a credible deterrence and defence posture. This means that NATO must continue to have the military strength needed to deter any attack, and to defend all of its members should an attack occur. NATO takes an active role in a broad range of crisis management operations and missionsopens in a new tab, in the Euro-Atlantic area and beyond. These activities range from peace support operations following conflicts, to capacity-building missions that help strengthen NATO’s partners, to humanitarian operations after natural disasters. NATO can conduct them alone, or in cooperation with other countries and international organisations. When the North Atlantic Council agrees to launch an operation, members contribute military forces on a voluntary basis. These forces then return to their countries once the mission is completed. NATO works with many non-member countries, called NATO partnersopens in a new tab, on a wide range of political and security-related issues. These countries pursue dialogue and practical cooperation with NATO and many contribute to NATO-led operations and missions. NATO also cooperates with a wide network of international organisationsopens in a new tab. Partner countries do not have the same decision-making authority as member countries and are not covered by the Article 5 collective defence commitment in NATO’s founding treaty. NATO has always innovated and adapted itself to ensure that its policies, capabilities and structures meet current and future threats, and continue to secure the collective defence of its members. NATO Allies are increasing their defence investments, developing the capabilities required to maintain NATO’s military edge in a changing security environment. Agencies × Member countries NATO has 32 member countriesopens in a new tab from Europe and North America. These sovereign states, called NATO Allies, come together through NATO to discuss political and security issues and make collective decisions by consensus. × National Delegations Each member country has a permanent delegationopens in a new tab at NATO’s political headquarters in Brussels, Belgium. Each delegation is headed by a Permanent Representative, who acts on behalf of his/her government in NATO’s consultation and decision-making process. × Military Representatives NATO’s Integrated Military Command Structure is composed of a number of key actors. At NATO Headquarters, each member country is represented by a senior military officer who serves as their country’s Military Representativeopens in a new tab (MILREP) on the Military Committee (MC) and acts on behalf of their respective Chief of Defence (CHOD). The MC convenes regularly to deliberate on issues of military significance, including in meetings at the level of the CHODs three times per year. × Nuclear Planning Group The Nuclear Planning Groupopens in a new tab (NPG) is the senior body on nuclear matters in NATO. It has the same authority as the North Atlantic Council with regard to nuclear policy issues. All member countries sit on the NPG, except France, which has decided not to participate. It is chaired by the NATO Secretary General and usually meets at the level of Defence Ministers. × North Atlantic Council The North Atlantic Councilopens in a new tab (NAC) is the principal political decision-making body at NATO. Each member country has a seat at the NAC. It meets at least once a week or whenever the need arises, at different levels. It is chaired by the Secretary General, who helps members reach agreement on key issues. × Subordinate Committees NATO has a network of committeesopens in a new tab to deal with all subjects on its agenda, from political to more technical issues. They bring together national representatives and experts from all NATO member countries on a regular basis. × Secretary General The Secretary Generalopens in a new tab is NATO’s top international civil servant. He steers the process of consultation and decision-making within NATO and ensures that decisions are implemented. The Secretary General is also NATO's chief spokesperson and heads the Organization's International Staff, who provide advice, guidance and administrative support to the national delegations at NATO Headquarters. × Military Committee The NATO Military Committeeopens in a new tab (MC) is NATO’s senior military authority. It serves as the essential link between the political decision-making process and NATO’s integrated military structure. The MC is composed of senior military officers from each NATO member state. The Committee is presided over by the Chair and is supported by the International Military Staff, its executive body. × Allied Command Transformation Allied Command Transformation (ACT) is one of the two Strategic Commands within NATO’s military command structure. Based in the United States, ACT leads NATO’s military adaptation, ensuring that Allied forces develop the right capabilities to maintain NATO’s warfighting edge. It is led by the Supreme Allied Commander Transformation (SACT). × Allied Command Operations Allied Command Operations (ACO) is one of the two Strategic Commands within NATO’s military command structure. Based in Belgium, ACO is responsible for the planning and execution of all NATO military operations. It is led by the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR). × Agencies NATO agencies and organisations play a vital role in procuring and sustaining capabilities collectively. They specialise in technical fields that complement and form an integral part of NATO’s agenda: procurement, support, and communications and information.
